            14       standard to requests to seal all or part of a complaint, meaning that there must be “compelling reasons

            15       supported by specific factual findings” to justify sealing. Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of Honolulu, 447

            16       F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (citation omitted); see, e.g., In re NVIDIA Corp. Derivative Litig.,

            17       2008 WL 1859067, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 23, 2008).

            18              Courts in this Circuit regularly find compelling reasons to seal nonpublic material contained in

            19       pleadings that reveals “confidential business information, the disclosure of which would cause

            20       competitive harm.” Actian Corp. v. AB Sciex LLC, 2023 WL 7166811, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 30, 2023);

            22       might harm a litigant’s competitive standing” provides basis for sealing.). The compelling reasons

Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Holdings LLC (d/b/a SecureSight) and RLDGroup, bring this putative class action against

                                  14   Defendants Automattic Inc. and Charles Matthew Mullenweg. Plaintiffs assert claims for

                                  15   intentional interference with contractual relations, intentional interference with prospective

                                  16   economic relations, and for violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law, Cal. Bus. & Profs.

                                  17   Code § 17200, based on alleged harm they suffered when Defendants blocked a third-party,

                                  18   WPEngine, Inc. (“WPE”), from accessing WordPress.org. Plaintiffs are WPE customers who rely

                                  19   on its hosting services to operate their own businesses, and deliver services to their own clients,

                                  20   within the WordPress ecosystem.

                                  21           Defendants move to dismiss Plaintiffs’ second amended complaint under Rule 12(b)(1) for

                                  22   lack of Article III standing and pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim. The motion

                                  23   is fully briefed and suitable for disposition without hearing pursuant to Civil Local Rule 7-1(b).

                                  24   Accordingly, the hearing currently set for July 30, 2026, is VACATED. Having reviewed the

                                  25   parties’ papers, the arguments therein, and the relevant legal authority, the Court DENIES the

                                  26   motion IN PART and GRANTS the motion IN PART for the reasons set forth below. This

                                  27   Order assumes familiarity with Plaintiffs’ factual allegations and the procedural history of this

                                  28   case.
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01892-AMO             Document 75         Filed 07/27/26      Page 2 of 11




                                   1                                               DISCUSSION

                                   2          The Court first takes up the threshold issue of Article III standing that Defendants raise

                                   3   under Rule 12(b)(1), before turning to those they raise under Rule 12(b)(6).

                                   4          A.      Article III Standing
                                   5          To establish standing under Article III of the Constitution, Plaintiffs “must show (i) that

                                   6   [they] suffered an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent; (ii) that the

                                   7   injury was likely caused by the defendant; and (iii) that the injury would likely be redressed by

                                   8   judicial relief.” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413, 423 (2021) (citing Lujan v. Defs. of

                                   9   Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560-61 (1992)). “[S]tanding is not dispensed in gross; rather, plaintiffs

                                  10   must demonstrate standing for each claim that they press and for each form of relief that they seek

                                  11   (for example, injunctive relief and damages).” Id. at 431 (citations omitted). “For injunctive

                                  12   relief, which is a prospective remedy, the threat of injury must be actual and imminent, not
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   conjectural or hypothetical.” Davidson v. Kimberly-Clark Corp., 889 F.3d 956, 967 (9th Cir.

                                  14   2018) (internal quotations and citation omitted). “Where standing is premised entirely on the

                                  15   threat of repeated injury, a plaintiff must show a sufficient likelihood that he will again be

                                  16   wronged in a similar way.” Id. (internal quotations and citation omitted).

                                  17          Defendants contend Plaintiffs have to establish Article III standing to assert any of their

                                  18   three claims. Dkt. No. 60 (“Mot.”) at 11-12. This argument fails as to Plaintiffs’ claims for

                                  19   monetary remedies. Plaintiffs allege they were denied the benefit of their bargain with WPE.

                                  20   Under the Scale Plan Keller purchased from WPE for the yearly fee of $3,300, he was entitled to

                                  21   “(i) automated WordPress and PHP updates, described as ‘effortless site management’; (ii)

                                  22   security patching and plugin risk scans; and (iii) fully managed WP, PHP, and MySQL updates.”

                                  23   Dkt. No. 57 (“SAC”) ¶ 73. All of these services required continuous access to WordPress.org. Id.

                                  24   When Defendants blocked WPE’s access to the platform, Plaintiff Keller had to perform all of

                                  25   these tasks himself, “which took significant time and expense.” Id. As a result of Defendants’

                                  26   actions, Plaintiff Keller did not receive the benefit of his bargain with WPE. Id. ¶ 76.

                                  27          Plaintiff Schanzer pays $762.12 per month for a Premium 1 Plan with WPE. Id. ¶ 87.

                                  28   That plan offers “(i) automated WordPress & PHP updates and ‘[e]ffortless site management with
                                                                                          2
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01892-AMO            Document 75        Filed 07/27/26       Page 3 of 11




                                   1   daily backups, one-click staging, automatic WordPress & PHP updates, and simple-to-use portal,’

                                   2   (ii) security patching and plugin risk scans, and (iii) fully managed WP, PHP & MySQL updates

                                   3   as well as access to themes[,]” all of which required continuous access to WordPress.org. Id.

                                   4   (modifications in original). When Defendants cut off WPE’s access to WordPress.org, Plaintiff

                                   5   Schanzer had to perform all of these functions herself, “which took significant time and expense.”

                                   6   Id. ¶ 90. She, like Plaintiff Keller, did not receive the benefit of her bargain due to Defendants’

                                   7   conduct. Id.

                                   8           These allegations plausibly plead a concrete economic injury,1 that is fairly traceable to

                                   9   Defendants’ conduct and redressable by this Court. This is sufficient to satisfy Article III standing

                                  10   requirements with respect to Plaintiffs’ claims for monetary remedies. See Williams v. Apple, Inc.,

                                  11   449 F. Supp. 3d 892, 905 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (“Generally, where plaintiffs plead that they were

                                  12   economically harmed because they did not receive the ‘benefit of the bargain,’ plaintiffs have
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   adequately alleged Article III standing”) (citations omitted). Defendants’ attack on this ground

                                  14   therefore fails.

                                  15           Defendants challenge to Plaintiffs’ Article III standing to seek injunctive relief, Mot. at 12,

                                  16   fares better. They argue that because the Court issued an injunction in the related case brought by

                                  17   WPE, “Plaintiffs lack standing for injunctive relief because they do not plausibly allege a ‘real and

                                  18   immediate threat of repeated injury.’ ” Id. (citing City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95, 102

                                  19   (1983)). Plaintiffs assert that, “[i]n the absence of a permanent injunction, Defendants will resume

                                  20   their attempts to harm WPE customers, and Plaintiffs ‘will have no option but to terminate their

                                  21   relationships with WPE because of the danger Defendants’ unlawful and unfair business practices

                                  22   pose.” Opp. at 27 (citing SAC ¶ 147). They contend “[e]quitable relief is particularly

                                  23   appropriate” given the findings in the related action, where the Court issued a preliminary

                                  24   injunction in part because maintaining “continuity and preventing arbitrary disruption stemming

                                  25   from a corporate dispute is in the public interest.” WPEngine, Inc. v. Automattic Inc., No. 24-CV-

                                  26
                                       1
                                  27     Plaintiffs also allege they incurred mitigation costs. SAC ¶¶ 68, 71, 84; Dkt. No. 62 (“Opp.”) at
                                       13. Because the lost benefit of their bargain with WPE is sufficient to confer standing, the Court
                                  28   thus does not reach the parties’ arguments about whether mitigation costs independently establish
                                       standing under Article III or statutory standing under the UCL.
                                                                                          3
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01892-AMO              Document 75         Filed 07/27/26     Page 4 of 11




                                   1   06917-AMO, 2024 WL 5077610, at *16 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 10, 2024). Here, Plaintiffs claim that

                                   2   without permanent equitable relief, “Defendants remain free to resume the same disruptive

                                   3   conduct that prompted the injunction—conduct that threatens ongoing harm to Plaintiffs, class

                                   4   members, and the broader WordPress ecosystem.” Opp. at 27. Plaintiffs, however, do not address

                                   5   how they face a “real and immediate threat of repeated injury” while the preliminary injunction

                                   6   issued in the related case remains in effect. See generally Opp. They have thus failed to establish

                                   7   standing to pursue injunctive relief in this action.

                                   8             Accordingly, Defendants’ motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction pursuant to Rule

                                   9   12(b)(1) is granted, with leave to amend, to the extent Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief. It is denied

                                  10   to the extent Plaintiffs seek monetary remedies. The Court now moves to grounds for dismissal

                                  11   that Defendants raise under Rule 12(b)(6) as to Plaintiffs’ intentional interference and UCL

                                  12   claims.

 United States District Court




                                  13             B.     Intentional Interference Claims
                                  14                    1.      Intentional Interference with Contractual Relations
                                  15             The elements of Plaintiffs’ claim for intentional interference with contractual relations are

                                  16   “(1) a valid contract between plaintiff and a third party; (2) defendant’s knowledge of this

                                  17   contract; (3) defendant’s intentional acts designed to induce a breach or disruption of the

                                  18   contractual relationship; (4) actual breach or disruption of the contractual relationship; and

                                  19   (5) resulting damage.” hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180, 1191 (9th Cir. 2022)

                                  20   (internal quotations and citation omitted).

                                  21             Defendants challenge the sufficiency of Plaintiffs’ allegations as to the elements of

                                  22   knowledge, intent, and breach or disruption. Mot. at 12-16. The Court analyzes each below.

                                  23                            a.      Knowledge
                                  24             Plaintiffs have sufficiently pleaded that Defendants knew about their contracts with WPE.

                                  25   As early as November 6, 2024, Defendants published a list of WPE customer websites. SAC

                                  26   ¶ 101. While Defendants claim that nothing on that list “indicates who owns those websites,”

                                  27   Mot. at 13, Plaintiffs allege that “the technical sophistication required to compile th[e] list

                                  28   demonstrates that Defendants had access and utilized data identifying specific WPE customers[,]”
                                                                                           4
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01892-AMO            Document 75        Filed 07/27/26      Page 5 of 11




                                   1   including “specific identifying information about which domains were hosted on WPE’s

                                   2   infrastructure.” SAC ¶ 101. Indeed, “Defendants had to identify WPE traffic to block it.” Id.

                                   3          The list contained 842,514 different WPE-hosted domains. Id. ¶ 101 “Every single

                                   4   website” that Plaintiff Schanzer “owned or operated appeared on the list.” Id. ¶ 103. Eighteen of

                                   5   the nineteen websites Plaintiff Keller operated appeared on the list. Id. Defendants “represented

                                   6   publicly that this list represented every domain hosted by WPE[] and that ‘you can see the decline

                                   7   every day’ for each day since September 21, 2024.” Id. ¶ 105. These were websites Defendants

                                   8   deemed “ready for a new home.” Id. ¶ 107. Defendants used the list to track how many

                                   9   customers WPE was losing each day, determine whether to provide or restrict access to

                                  10   WordPress.org depending on the website’s affiliation with WPE, track the sites that changed web

                                  11   hosts each day (down to the minute), and to poach specific WPE customers. Id. ¶¶ 101, 106, 107,

                                  12   110, 112.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          While Plaintiffs do not allege that Defendants tried to poach them specifically, Plaintiffs

                                  14   have pleaded sufficient facts to support a reasonable inference that Defendants knew they had

                                  15   contracts with WPE.2 As Plaintiffs themselves note, “Defendants would not have published

                                  16   Plaintiffs’ websites on their own WPE customer list if they did not believe that Plaintiffs were

                                  17   WPE customers.” Id. ¶ 108. Defendants may challenge whether the WPE customer list actually

                                  18   conveys the information necessary to prove knowledge at a later stage. Moore v. Apple, Inc., 73 F.

                                  19   Supp. 3d 1191, 1203 (N.D. Cal. 2014) (finding allegation that wireless service providers update

                                  20   wireless accounts when users switch from Apple to non-Apple devices sufficient to establish

                                  21   support an inference of knowledge and noting “Defendant may contest whether the wireless

                                  22   providers’ update or Plaintiff’s contact with Apple personnel actually conveyed the relevant

                                  23   information to Apple”). For now, the existing allegations in the second amended complaint are

                                  24   sufficient to establish knowledge for purposes of the Plaintiffs’ intentional interference with

                                  25   contractual relations claim. See id.

                                  26
                                       2
                                  27     To the extent Defendants contend Plaintiffs have failed to allege that Defendants had knowledge
                                       about the specifics of their contracts with WPE, Mot. at 13-14, that is not grounds for dismissal at
                                  28   the pleading stage. See Moore, 73 F. Supp. 3d at 1203 (rejecting the argument that the plaintiff
                                       had to identify a specific contract term or language).

                                                              b.     Intent
                                   1
                                              Plaintiffs have also sufficiently pleaded intent. Defendants disabled WPE’s access to
                                   2
                                       WordPress.org, which Defendants knew would degrade WPE’s services, and consequently, those
                                   3
                                       of its customers, including Plaintiffs. SAC ¶ 55. The goal of their “scorched earth nuclear war”
                                   4
                                       against WPE, id. ¶ 100, was to “deliberately target[] and inhibit[] the services and contracts
                                   5
                                       between WPE and Plaintiffs and Class Members.” Id. ¶ 56. “[I]mmediately after the disruptions
                                   6
                                       to WPE began,” Defendants’ “sales representatives began contacting WPE customers.” Id. ¶ 60;
                                   7
                                       see also id. ¶ 59. While Defendants describe this behavior as demonstrating “at most an intent to
                                   8
                                       compete for business,” Mot. at 15, the Court must take Plaintiffs allegations as true and draw all
                                   9
                                       inferences in their favor. See Gregg v. Hawaii Dep’t of Pub. Safety, 870 F.3d 883, 887 (9th Cir.
                                  10
                                       2017). On the current allegations then, Plaintiffs have plausibly established that Defendants acted
                                  11
                                       intentionally with the aim of disruption and inducing breach of their contracts with WPE. See
                                  12
Northern District of California




                                       Moore, 73 F. Supp. 3d at 1203 (finding intent sufficiently pleaded where plaintiff alleged that
 United States District Court




                                  13
                                       “Apple, as designer of the Messages application, knew that use of iMessages would result in
                                  14
                                       undelivered text messages if a user switched to a non-Apple device” but failed to alert consumers
                                  15
                                       about the issue).

                                                              c.     Breach or Disruption
                                  17
                                              Plaintiffs’ allegations of disruption are also sufficient. The benefits for which Plaintiffs
                                  18
                                       contracted with WPE required continued access to WordPress.org. SAC ¶¶ 73, 90. By cutting off
                                  19
                                       WPE’s access, Plaintiffs “were unable to install or update Plugins or themes[,]” their
                                  20
                                       administrative access to the websites they operated was limited, as “they could not update the
                                  21
                                       Plugins, themes, and in some cases the content of the website,” and they had “limited access to
                                  22
                                       software updates, editing tools, and access control because these features were all tied to the
                                  23
                                       WordPress central repository.” Id. ¶ 48. This “crippled website owners’ ability to control and
                                  24
                                       modify their websites in a managed environment, as they had paid WPE for[.]” Id. It also
                                  25
                                       “created a significant security risk, as security vulnerabilities may not be left unpatched.” Id. As a
                                  26
                                       result, Plaintiffs had to perform the services they had contracted for themselves, leaving them
                                  27
                                       without the benefit of the contracts they had negotiated with WPE. Id. ¶¶ 76, 90. While
                                  28
                                                                                         6
                                        Case 4:25-cv-01892-AMO            Document 75          Filed 07/27/26     Page 7 of 11




                                   1   Defendants urge the Court to require Plaintiffs to identify the relevant terms of their actual

                                   2   contracts with WPE and show how Defendants prevented performance or made performance more

                                   3   expensive or difficult, Mot. at 15-16, Plaintiffs’ allegations adequately establish disruption at the

                                   4   pleading stage. See Moore, 73 F. Supp. 3d at 1204 (finding element of breach or disruption

                                   5   sufficiently pleaded where plaintiff alleged Apple’s Messages application prevented her from

                                   6   receiving text messages, a service for which Plaintiff paid as part of her wireless service contract).

                                   7                  2.      Intentional Interference with Prospective Economic Relations
                                   8          The elements of Plaintiffs’ claim for intentional interference with prospective economic

                                  11   relationship; (3) intentional acts on the part of the defendant designed to disrupt the relationship;

                                  12   (4) actual disruption of the relationship; and (5) economic harm to the plaintiff proximately caused

                                  13   by the acts of the defendant.” CRST Van Expedited, Inc. v. Werner Enters., Inc., 479 F.3d 1099,

                                  14   1108 (9th Cir. 2007) (citing Korea Supply Co. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 29 Cal. 4th 1134, 1153

                                  15   (2003)).

                                  16          Defendants argue this claim fails for lack of sufficient allegations of the requisite economic

                                  17   relationship, defendant’s knowledge, or independent wrongful acts. Mot. at 18. As before,

                                  18   assuming Plaintiffs adequately plead the remaining elements of this claim, their allegations do not

                                  20   probability of future economic benefit to the plaintiff.” See CRST Van Expedited, Inc., 479 F.3d at

                                  24   falls short of suggesting a “reasonabl[e] probab[ility] that the prospective economic advantage

                                  15          Under the UCL’s “the narrower standing requirements[,]” a party must “(1) establish a loss

                                  16   or deprivation of money or property sufficient to qualify as injury in fact, i.e., economic injury,

                                  17   and (2) show that that economic injury was the result of, i.e., caused by, the unfair business

                                  19   Cal. 4th 310, 322 (2011).

                                  21   Mot. at 19. Plaintiffs counter that because they have “alleged a direct economic injury—the loss

                                  27   standing for the reasons previously discussed in this Order. Defendants’ motion to dismiss the

                                   7   an unfair business practice to those persons in interest from whom the property was taken, that is,
